title: Coordinate Geometry
short: Distance formula, section formula, area of a triangle.
lede: Three formulas, six marks, no surprises. Finish this unit early and bank it.
lens: Typical questions: distance between two points, a point dividing a segment in a given ratio, finding an unknown coordinate from a given distance, and area of a triangle or collinearity.
concepts: **1. Distance formula.** The distance between (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) is `√[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²]` — just Pythagoras.
**2. Section formula.** The point dividing the segment joining (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) internally in the ratio m:n is `((mx₂ + nx₁)/(m+n), (my₂ + ny₁)/(m+n))`.
**3. Midpoint** is the section formula with m:n = 1:1.
**4. Centroid** of a triangle is the average of the three vertices’ coordinates.
**5. Area of a triangle.** `(1/2)|x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂)|`. If this comes out as 0, the three points are **collinear**.
tricks: - **Section formula cross pattern:** m goes with the *second* point’s coordinates and n with the first. Write it out once correctly and reuse it.
- **Equidistant point problems:** set the two distances equal and **square both sides immediately** to remove the roots.
- **Collinearity** is the same calculation as area = 0. Do not learn it as a separate method.
- A point on the x-axis has y = 0; a point on the y-axis has x = 0. Substituting that first halves the working.
mistakes: - Mixing up which ratio component multiplies which point in the section formula.
- Forgetting the modulus in the area formula, then reporting a negative area.
- Sign errors with negative coordinates: (x₂ − x₁) with x₁ negative becomes addition.
- Leaving the distance as an unsimplified surd when an exact value is wanted.

qa.q: Find the distance between (−2, 3) and (4, −5).
qa.a: Using the distance formula d = √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²]: d = √[(4 − (−2))² + (−5 − 3)²] = √[36 + 64] = √100 = **10 units**. Note the signs: subtracting a negative coordinate becomes an addition, and both differences are squared, so it does not matter which point is taken first.

qa.q: Find the point that divides the segment joining (−1, 7) and (4, −3) in the ratio 2:3.
a: The point is (1, 3).

qa.q: Find a relation between x and y if the point (x, y) is equidistant from (3, 6) and (−3, 4).
a: Set the squared distances equal: (x−3)² + (y−6)² = (x+3)² + (y−4)².
Expanding and cancelling x² and y²: −6x − 12y + 45 = 6x − 8y + 25.
So 12x + 4y = 20, that is 3x + y = 5.

qa.q: Find the area of the triangle with vertices (1, −1), (−4, 2k) and (−k, 5) if the area is 24/2 square units.
a: So 2k² + 3k − 29 = ±24, giving 2k² + 3k − 53 = 0 or 2k² + 3k − 5 = 0.
The second factorises as (2k + 5)(k − 1) = 0, so k = 1 or k = −5/2. Always keep both the + and − cases because of the modulus.

qa.q: A student finds the distance between A(−3, 2) and B(5, −4) as √[(5 − 3)² + (−4 − 2)²] = √40. Find the error and give the correct distance.
a: Error: x₂ − x₁ = 5 − (−3) = 5 + 3 = **8**, not 2. The negative sign of x₁ was dropped.

qa.q: A petrol station is to be built on the road along the x-axis so that it is equidistant from two villages at P(2, −5) and Q(−2, 9). Find the coordinates of the station.
a: Let the station be S(x, 0). Then SP = SQ, so SP² = SQ².
So −8x = 56 and x = −7. The station is at **(−7, 0)**.

qa.q: Find the ratio in which the point (−1, 6) divides the line segment joining (−3, 10) and (6, −8).
a: Let the ratio be k : 1. Using the section formula on x: −1 = (6k − 3)/(k + 1).
⇒ −k − 1 = 6k − 3 ⇒ 7k = 2 ⇒ k = 2/7, so the ratio is 2 : 7.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

On a grid map, a school is at S(−2, 1) and a library is at L(6, 7). A bus stop M is to be placed exactly midway between them, and a park is at P(2, −2).

(a) Find the distance SL.
(b) Find the coordinates of M.
(c) Find the distance MP.

Read and answer:

Three vertices of a parallelogram ABCD, taken in order, are A(1, 2), B(4, 3) and C(6, 6).

(a) Find the coordinates of D.
(b) Verify your answer using the diagonals.
(c) Which property of a parallelogram did you use?
a: (a) The diagonals AC and BD bisect each other. Midpoint of AC = (7/2, 4). If D = (x, y), midpoint of BD = ((4 + x)/2, (3 + y)/2) = (7/2, 4), so x = 3 and y = 5. D = **(3, 5)**.
(b) Check: vector AB = (3, 1) and vector DC = (6 − 3, 6 − 5) = (3, 1), so AB and DC are equal and parallel ✓.
(c) The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, so they share the same midpoint.

qa.q: Find the area of the quadrilateral with vertices (−4, −2), (−3, −5), (3, −2) and (2, 3), taken in order.
a: Split it along the diagonal AC into ΔABC and ΔACD.
Total area = 10.5 + 17.5 = 28 sq units.

qa.q: Show that the points (1, 7), (4, 2), (−1, −1) and (−4, 4) are the vertices of a square.
a: Diagonals: AC = √(4 + 64) = √68 and BD = √(64 + 4) = √68 — equal.
A quadrilateral with all four sides equal and equal diagonals is a square.

qa.q: Find the ratio in which the y-axis divides the line segment joining A(5, −6) and B(−1, −4). Also find the point of division.
a: A point on the y-axis has x = 0. Let it divide AB in the ratio k : 1.
The y-axis meets AB at **(0, −13/3)**.

mcq.q: The distance of the point (3, 4) from the origin is: (a) 5  (b) 7  (c) 25  (d) 12
Three points are collinear if the area of the triangle they form is: (a) 1  (b) maximum  (c) 0  (d) negative
The coordinates of the point that divides the line segment joining (0, 0) and (6, 9) internally in the ratio 1 : 2 are: (a) (3, 9/2)  (b) (4, 6)  (c) (2, 3)  (d) (1, 3/2)
The area of the triangle with vertices (0, 0), (4, 0) and (0, 3) is: (a) 6 square units  (b) 12 square units  (c) 7 square units  (d) 3.5 square units
mcq.a: **(a) 6 square units.** It is right-angled at the origin, so the area is ½ × 4 × 3 = 6 square units.

mcq.q: The point (−3, 0) lies on: (a) the x-axis  (b) the y-axis  (c) the line y = x  (d) the origin
mcq.a: **(a) the x-axis.** Every point whose y-coordinate is 0 lies on the x-axis.

mcq.q: The distance of (a cos θ, a sin θ) from the origin is: (a) a  (b) a²  (c) 1  (d) 2a
The centroid of the triangle with vertices (2, 3), (−4, 7) and (2, −4) is: (a) (0, 2)  (b) (0, 0)  (c) (2, 2)  (d) (0, 3)

trend: One 3-mark question on the section formula or an equidistant relation, plus objective questions on distance and midpoint.
onepager: - Section: m pairs with the second point.
task: Plot three points on graph paper, measure the side lengths with a ruler, then compute them with the distance formula. The comparison makes it obvious why the formula works.
steps: 1. Write every point as **(x, y)** and mark roughly where it lies — a quick sketch catches sign errors before they reach the formula.
2. For a distance use **d = √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²]**; for a midpoint use **((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2)**. Keep the differences in brackets until you have squared them.
3. For a section, apply the **section formula** with m : n in the order given: ((mx₂ + nx₁)/(m + n), (my₂ + ny₁)/(m + n)). For a trisection, take m : n as 1 : 2 then 2 : 1.
4. For collinearity, check that the **area of the triangle is zero**, or that the slopes of all three pairs match — state which test you used.

title: Introduction to Trigonometry
short: Trigonometric ratios, the standard table and identities.
lede: The ratio table unlocks this chapter and the next one. Learn it cold.
lens: Roughly **7–8 of the 12 Trigonometry marks**. Identities are worth 3 marks and are asked as proofs.
Objective questions on the standard values (0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°) are near-certain.
concepts: **1. The six ratios.** In a right triangle with respect to an acute angle θ: sin = opposite/hypotenuse, cos = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan = opposite/adjacent. The other three are their reciprocals: cosec, sec, cot.
**2. Trigonometric identities.** `sin²A + cos²A = 1` for all A; `1 + tan²A = sec²A` and `1 + cot²A = cosec²A` for A ≠ 90°.
**3. Complementary angles.** `sin(90° − A) = cos A`, `cos(90° − A) = sin A`, `tan(90° − A) = cot A`, and similarly for the reciprocals.
**4. Proving identities.** Always start from the more complicated side and transform it into the other. Never work on both sides at once — that is not a valid proof.
formulas: sin(90° − A) = cos A,  cos(90° − A) = sin A
tan θ = sin θ / cos θ,  cot θ = 1/tan θ
tricks: - **Building the sin table:** write 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 under 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°, divide each by 4, then take the square root. The cos row is the sin row read backwards.
- **SOH CAH TOA** for the three primary ratios.
- For a proof, convert everything to sin and cos first. Almost every identity collapses after that.
- If a question gives sin A = 3/5 and asks for the other ratios, draw the right triangle and read them off — do not reach for identities.
mistakes: - In proofs, manipulating both sides until they match. Start from one side only.
- Forgetting the condition A ≠ 90° when using the tan and cot identities.
- Confusing sin(90° − A) with sin 90° − A. The parentheses matter.

qa.q: Evaluate sin 60° cos 30° + cos 60° sin 30°.
If sin A = 3/5, find cos A and tan A (A is acute).
a: Draw the right triangle: opposite = 3, hypotenuse = 5, so adjacent = √(25 − 9) = 4.
cos A = 4/5 and tan A = 3/4.

qa.q: If tan θ = 5/12, find sin θ and cos θ.
qa.a: Take the perpendicular as 5k and the base as 12k, so the hypotenuse is √(25 + 144)k = 13k. Hence sin θ = 5/13 and cos θ = 12/13.

qa.q: Prove that (1 + tan²A)/(1 + cot²A) = tan²A.
a: Start from the left-hand side.
1 + tan²A = sec²A and 1 + cot²A = cosec²A.
So LHS = sec²A / cosec²A = (1/cos²A) ÷ (1/sin²A) = sin²A/cos²A = tan²A = RHS.

qa.q: If tan(A + B) = √3 and tan(A − B) = 1/√3, with 0° < A + B ≤ 90° and A > B, find A and B.
a: tan(A + B) = √3 gives A + B = 60°.
tan(A − B) = 1/√3 gives A − B = 30°.
Adding: 2A = 90°, so A = 45° and B = 15°.

qa.q: A student simplifies sin(90° − 30°) as sin 90° − sin 30° = 1 − 1/2 = 1/2. What is wrong? Give the correct value and check it a second way.
a: sin(A − B) is **not** sin A − sin B; sine does not distribute over a bracket. The angle inside the brackets must be simplified first.
Check with the complementary-angle identity: sin(90° − A) = cos A, so sin 60° = cos 30° = √3/2 ✓.

qa.q: If 7 sin²θ + 3 cos²θ = 4 and θ is acute, show that tan θ = 1/√3.
a: Write 7 sin²θ + 3 cos²θ = 3(sin²θ + cos²θ) + 4 sin²θ = 3 + 4 sin²θ.
So 3 + 4 sin²θ = 4, which gives sin²θ = 1/4 and sin θ = 1/2 (θ acute), so θ = 30°.
Hence tan θ = tan 30° = **1/√3**.

qa.q: Prove that (cosec A − sin A)(sec A − cos A) = 1/(tan A + cot A).
a: LHS = (1/sin A − sin A)(1/cos A − cos A) = [(1 − sin²A)/sin A] × [(1 − cos²A)/cos A]
= (cos²A/sin A) × (sin²A/cos A) = sin A cos A.
RHS = 1/[(sin A/cos A) + (cos A/sin A)] = 1/[(sin²A + cos²A)/(sin A cos A)] = sin A cos A.
LHS = RHS, so the identity is proved.

qa.q: Prove that √[(1 + sin A)/(1 − sin A)] = sec A + tan A.
a: Multiply inside the root by (1 + sin A)/(1 + sin A): √[(1 + sin A)²/(1 − sin²A)] = √[(1 + sin A)²/cos²A].
= (1 + sin A)/cos A = 1/cos A + sin A/cos A = sec A + tan A.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

Riya notices from the standard table that sin 30° = cos 60° = 1/2, sin 45° = cos 45° = 1/√2 and sin 60° = cos 30° = √3/2.

(a) Which relation connects each pair of values?
(b) Use it to evaluate sin 65° ÷ cos 25° and tan 35° × tan 55°.
(c) Why does the table not list a value for tan 90°?
a: (a) The angles in each pair are complementary: sin(90° − θ) = cos θ.
(b) sin 65° = sin(90° − 25°) = cos 25°, so the ratio is **1**. tan 55° = cot 35°, so tan 35° × tan 55° = tan 35° × cot 35° = **1**.
(c) tan 90° = sin 90°/cos 90° = 1/0, which is not defined.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

Meera claims that sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 is true for every angle and that 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ is true for every angle too.

(a) For which angle from 0° to 90° is her second claim meaningless?
(b) Derive 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ from sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.
(c) If sec θ = 5/3 and θ is acute, find tan θ.
a: (a) At θ = 90°, where cos θ = 0, tan θ and sec θ are not defined.
(b) Divide sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 by cos²θ (cos θ ≠ 0): tan²θ + 1 = sec²θ.

qa.q: Prove that (sin θ + cosec θ)² + (cos θ + sec θ)² = 7 + tan²θ + cot²θ.
a: LHS = sin²θ + cosec²θ + 2 sin θ cosec θ + cos²θ + sec²θ + 2 cos θ sec θ.
Since sin θ cosec θ = 1 and cos θ sec θ = 1, the two middle terms give 2 + 2 = 4.
So LHS = (sin²θ + cos²θ) + 4 + cosec²θ + sec²θ = 1 + 4 + (1 + cot²θ) + (1 + tan²θ).
= 7 + tan²θ + cot²θ = RHS. ∎

mcq.q: The value of cos 60° is: (a) 1/2  (b) √3/2  (c) 1/√2  (d) 1
sin²30° + cos²30° equals: (a) 0  (b) 1/2  (c) 1  (d) 3/4
tan 45° × cot 45° is: (a) 0  (b) 1  (c) 2  (d) undefined
If cos A = 4/5 and A is acute, then tan A is: (a) 3/4  (b) 4/3  (c) 3/5  (d) 5/3
Which of the following is NOT defined? (a) tan 90°  (b) sin 90°  (c) cos 0°  (d) cot 90°
mcq.a: **(a) tan 90°.** tan 90° = sin 90°/cos 90° = 1/0. The others are 1, 1 and 0.

mcq.q: The value of sin²60° + 2 tan²45° − cos²30° is: (a) 1  (b) 2  (c) 5/4  (d) 9/4
If sin θ = cos θ, then θ = : (a) 0°  (b) 30°  (c) 45°  (d) 90°
sec²A − tan²A equals: (a) 0  (b) 1  (c) −1  (d) sin²A
mcq.a: **(b) 1.** It follows directly from 1 + tan²A = sec²A.

trend: One identity proof (3 marks) most years, plus objective questions on standard values and complementary angles.
onepager: - sin² + cos² = 1; 1 + tan² = sec²; 1 + cot² = cosec².
- Proofs: work from one side only.
task: Produce the sin–cos table from memory three times in a row. Then prove each of the three identities starting from the harder side.
steps: 1. Write the **six ratios** in terms of sides of a right triangle and fix the standard values for 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90° before attempting the sum.
2. Convert every ratio to **sin and cos**, then use **sin²θ + cos²θ = 1**, **1 + tan²θ = sec²θ** and **1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ** to simplify.
3. Use the **complementary angle** relations — sin(90° − θ) = cos θ, tan(90° − θ) = cot θ — whenever two angles in the question add to 90°.
4. Verify the **identity from one side to the other**; never start by assuming both sides are equal. End by naming the identity used.

title: Some Applications of Trigonometry
short: Heights and distances — angle of elevation and depression.
lede: One diagram, drawn correctly, answers nearly every question here.
lens: The remaining **4–5 marks of the 12-mark Trigonometry unit**.
Almost always a 3–4 mark word problem. The CBSE syllabus restricts this to two right triangles — no more than two lines of sight.
concepts: **1. Line of sight** is the line from the observer’s eye to the object being observed.
**2. Angle of elevation** is the angle the line of sight makes with the horizontal when the object is **above** the horizontal.

**3. Angle of depression** is the angle the line of sight makes with the horizontal when the object is **below** the horizontal. Measured from the horizontal at the observer’s end, never from the vertical.
**4. Method.** Draw the right triangle, mark the given angle, choose the ratio that involves the known side and the unknown side, then solve. Only 30°, 45° and 60° are used in the board paper.
steps: 1. Draw the diagram **before writing anything else**. Mark the observer, the horizontal and the object.
2. If the observer has height, subtract it: the triangle starts at eye level, not ground level.
3. Label the known side and the unknown side.
4. Pick the ratio involving both — almost always tan.
5. Solve, then add back any height you subtracted, and give the answer with units.
tricks: - **Angle of depression equals the angle of elevation from the other end** (alternate angles). So a depression problem becomes an elevation problem on a mirrored triangle.
- √3 ≈ 1.732 is usually given in the question. If the answer is expected as `10√3`, leave it as a surd unless told otherwise.
- If the problem has two angles from two positions, you get two equations in the same height. Equate them.
- “From the foot” of a tower means the horizontal distance starts at the base.
mistakes: - Measuring the angle of depression from the vertical.
- Forgetting to add the observer’s eye height back to the final answer.
- Using the wrong pair of sides in the ratio — check which side is opposite the marked angle.
- Drawing the horizontal from the object instead of from the observer.

qa.q: The angle of elevation of the top of a tower from a point 30 m from its foot is 60°. Find the height of the tower.
qa.a: In the right triangle, tan 60° = height ÷ distance, so √3 = h/30 and **h = 30√3 m ≈ 51.96 m**. Draw the triangle first — the tower is the perpendicular, the 30 m ground distance is the base, and the angle of elevation is at the foot. Unless asked for a decimal, 30√3 m is the exact answer and is preferred.

qa.q: From the top of a 75 m high lighthouse, the angles of depression of two ships on the same side are 30° and 45°. Find the distance between the ships.
a: For the ship at 45°: tan 45° = 75/x, so x = 75 m.
For the ship at 30°: tan 30° = 75/y, so y = 75√3 m.

qa.q: A boy whose eyes are 1.5 m above the ground stands 20√3 m from a tower and sees its top at an angle of elevation of 30°. He calculates the height as 20√3 × tan 30° = 20 m and stops. What is missing? Give the correct height.
a: The calculation gives only the height of the tower **above his eye level**; the 1.5 m from the ground to his eyes must be added back.
Height above eye level = 20√3 × (1/√3) = 20 m.
Height of the tower = 20 + 1.5 = **21.5 m**.

qa.q: A 20 m long ladder leans against a wall and makes an angle of 60° with the ground. How high up the wall does it reach, and how far is its foot from the wall? (Take √3 = 1.73.)
a: In the right triangle, the ladder is the hypotenuse: height = 20 sin 60° = 20 × √3/2 = 10√3.
Distance of the foot from the wall = 20 cos 60° = 20 × 1/2 = **10 m**.

qa.q: The shadow of a tower is 20 m longer when the sun’s elevation is 30° than when it is 60°. Find the height of the tower.
a: Let the height be h. Shadow at 60° = h/tan 60° = h/√3; shadow at 30° = h/tan 30° = h√3.

qa.q: Two poles of heights 6 m and 11 m stand upright on level ground with their feet 12 m apart. Find the distance between their tops.
a: The difference in height is 11 − 6 = 5 m and the horizontal gap is 12 m.
Distance between the tops = √(5² + 12²) = √169 = 13 m.

qa.q: A kite flies with 100 m of string out so that its height above the ground is 50 m. If the string is taut, find the angle of elevation of the kite.
a: Let the angle of elevation be θ. The string is the hypotenuse (100 m) and the height is the opposite side (50 m).
Therefore θ = 30°. The angle of elevation of the kite is 30°.

qa.q: A person on the bank of a river sees the top of a tree on the opposite bank at an angle of elevation of 60°. Walking 20 m away from the bank, the angle becomes 30°. Find the height of the tree and the width of the river.
a: Let the height be h and the width x.
From the nearer point: h = x√3. From the farther point: h = (x + 20)/√3.
Equating: x√3 = (x + 20)/√3, so 3x = x + 20 and x = 10 m.
Therefore h = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 m and the river is 10 m wide.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

From the top of a 12 m high building, the angle of elevation of the top of a cable tower is 60° and the angle of depression of its foot is 30°.

(a) Find the horizontal distance between the building and the tower.
(b) Find the height of the tower.
(c) Which of the two given angles is measured below the horizontal?
a: (a) Angle of depression of the foot is 30°: tan 30° = 12/d, so d = 12√3 m ≈ **20.8 m**.
(b) Above the building’s top: tan 60° = (H − 12)/d, so H − 12 = √3 × 12√3 = 36 and H = **48 m**.
(c) The 30° **angle of depression**, measured below the horizontal through the observer’s eye.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

A drone hovers 60 m above a straight road. Two observers A and B stand on the road on opposite sides of the point directly below the drone. They see it at angles of elevation 30° and 60° respectively.

(a) How far is A from the point below the drone?
(b) How far is B from that point?
(c) What is the distance AB? (Take √3 = 1.73.)
From a point 40 m from the foot of a tower the angle of elevation of its top is 30°. After hoisting a flag on top, the angle of elevation of the top of the flag is 45°. Find the height of the flag.
a: Height of the tower = 40 tan 30° = 40/√3 ≈ 23.1 m.
Height of tower + flag = 40 tan 45° = 40 m.

qa.q: The angles of elevation of the top of a tower from two points at distances 4 m and 9 m from its base, on the same straight line with the base, are complementary. Prove that the height of the tower is 6 m.
a: Let the tower be h m high. Let the angle of elevation from the point 4 m away be θ; from the point 9 m away it is (90° − θ).
From the nearer point: tan θ = h/4.
From the farther point: tan(90° − θ) = cot θ = h/9.
Multiply: tan θ × cot θ = (h/4)(h/9), so 1 = h²/36.
Hence h² = 36 and h = **6 m**. ∎

mcq.q: The angle of depression is always measured from: (a) the vertical  (b) the horizontal  (c) the object  (d) the ground below
mcq.a: **(b) The horizontal** at the observer’s end.

mcq.q: If the angle of elevation of the sun is 45°, the length of the shadow of a pole equals: (a) half its height  (b) its height  (c) twice its height  (d) √3 times its height
From the top of a tower the angle of depression of an object on the ground is 30°. The angle of elevation of the top from that object is: (a) 30°  (b) 45°  (c) 60°  (d) 90°
If the angle of elevation of the top of a pole from a point 10 m from its foot is 60°, the height of the pole is: (a) 10/√3 m  (b) 10 m  (c) 10√3 m  (d) 20 m
As an observer walks towards the foot of a tower, the angle of elevation of its top: (a) decreases  (b) stays the same  (c) becomes zero  (d) increases
mcq.a: **(d) increases.** The horizontal distance falls while the height stays fixed, so tan of the angle (height ÷ distance) grows and the angle increases.

mcq.q: When the shadow of a pole equals its height, the sun’s angle of elevation is: (a) 30°  (b) 45°  (c) 60°  (d) 90°
The angle made by the line of sight with the horizontal when the object is below the observer is the angle of: (a) elevation  (b) depression  (c) reflection  (d) inclination
mcq.a: **(b) depression.** Elevation looks up; depression looks down.

mcq.q: A 10 m ladder reaches a window 8 m above the ground. Its foot is from the wall at a distance of: (a) 4 m  (b) 6 m  (c) 7 m  (d) 9 m

trend: One 3–4 mark heights-and-distances problem each year. Two-position problems (walking away) are the common harder variant.
onepager: - Depression angle = elevation angle from the other end.
- Add the observer’s height back at the end.
task: Measure the shadow of a pole or a wall, then compute the height using the sun’s angle of elevation. Compare it with a tape measurement if you can.
